problem: Instruction-generation (speaker) models for language-based navigation produce instructions for a given trajectory naively, without optimizing which trajectory yields the best instruction in terms of length, perplexity and efficiency.
motivation: Good natural-language navigation instructions matter for human-robot interaction and for generating training data. The paper treats the choice of trajectory as an optimization problem over instruction quality, solved with a heuristic search. Only the abstract is available, so details are limited.
key_idea: Use genetic algorithms with modified crossover and mutation operators to search for trajectories in an environment that yield the best natural-language navigation instructions, scored by path length, instruction length, perplexity and efficiency.
insight: According to the abstract, genetic algorithms with modified crossover and mutation operators produce near-human-quality instructions and outperform naively generating instructions for a given trajectory. In some cases they yield shorter instructions of similar quality than human planning. No ablations can be cited because only the abstract is available.
method: Genetic algorithm search: evolves candidate trajectories through a test environment to optimize instruction quality
Fitness function: combines path length, instruction length, instruction perplexity and efficiency
Modified crossover and mutation operators: adapted to trajectory (path) representations
Instruction source: a dataset of navigation instructions is used to generate/interpolate instructions for novel trajectories

setting.backbone: Not specified in the abstract (a language model is used to score perplexity)
setting.training_data: A dataset of navigation instructions (not specified in the abstract)
setting.action_space: trajectory selection over an environment (not specified)

results: The abstract reports qualitatively that GA-optimized instructions are near-human quality and better than naive instruction generation for a given trajectory. In some cases they are shorter than human-planned instructions at similar quality. No numeric results are given.
limitations: Only the abstract is available, so datasets, models and numbers are unknown
Evaluation appears to be on a small test environment; generalization is unclear
compares_to: Naive instruction generation for a given trajectory
